# John C. Bogle: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing (2007)

Source: [The Little Book of Common Sense Investing](../../../../../The%20Little%20Book%20of%20Common%20Sense%20Investing_%20The%20Only%20Way%20to%20Guarantee%20Your%20Fair%20Share%20of%20Stock%20Mar...%7BJohn%20C.%20Bogle%7D%282007%29%7B91574839%7D%20libgen.li.md)

## 1. The Relentless Rules of Humble Arithmetic [verified]

- **Winner's game vs loser's game:** owning the whole market over the long term is a winner's game. *Beating* the market after costs is a loser's game, because investors as a group earn the market return *minus* costs.
- "Market return, minus cost, equals investor return."
- **Gotrocks parable:** a family owning all U.S. businesses earns everything those businesses earn. "Helpers" (brokers, managers, consultants) persuade family members to trade among themselves, and the family's share shrinks by every fee and tax paid. Solution: "Get rid of all your Helpers."
- "We investors as a group get precisely what we don't pay for. So if we pay nothing, we get everything."
- Paraphrasing Upton Sinclair: "It's amazing how difficult it is for a man to understand something if he's paid a small fortune not to understand it." This is incentive bias in the advice industry.

## 2. Where Stock Returns Come From [verified]

- **Investment return** = dividend yield + earnings growth. Historically about 9.5% (≈4.5% dividends + ≈5% earnings growth), or ≈6.5% real.
- **Speculative return** = change in the P/E multiple. It swings wildly by decade but nets close to zero over very long periods (reversion to the mean).
- Over the long run, market returns depend almost entirely on business fundamentals, not on changes in valuation.
- **Forecast method:** expected return ≈ current dividend yield + expected earnings growth ± expected P/E change. Subtract costs and inflation to get the real net return.

## 3. Costs: The Tyranny of Compounding [verified]

- Typical active equity fund (2007 data):
  - Expense ratio: ≈1.5%/yr
  - Sales charges: ≈0.5%/yr (a 5% load spread over 10 years; 1%/yr if held 5 years)
  - Hidden turnover costs: ≈1%/yr, at 100% turnover. Rule of thumb: **turnover costs ≈ 1% × the turnover rate**.
  - Opportunity cost of cash drag: about +0.3%/yr
  - **All-in cost: up to 3–3.5%/yr**
- **Example:** at 8% market returns for 50 years, $10,000 grows to **$469,000**. At 5.5% (after 2.5% costs) it grows to **$145,400**. Costs consume nearly 70% of the potential accumulation. The investor put up 100% of the capital and took 100% of the risk, yet got only 31% of the return.
- "The miracle of compounding returns is overwhelmed by the tyranny of compounding costs."
- "Where returns are concerned, time is your friend. But where costs are concerned, time is your enemy."
- **1980–2005 real-world gap:** the S&P 500 returned 12.5%/yr. The average fund returned 10.0%. An S&P 500 index fund returned 12.3% (costs about 0.2%).
- Taxes and inflation are additional costs. Index funds' low turnover makes them tax-efficient (see §4).

## 4. Taxes Are Costs, Too [verified]

- "Managed mutual funds are astonishingly tax-inefficient." Average equity-fund turnover is about **100%/yr** (61% asset-weighted), so the average stock is held about 12 months. From 1945 to 1965, turnover averaged just 16%, a six-year holding period.
- **1980–2005 tax drag** (federal only, taxable accounts): active funds ≈ **1.8 points/yr**, cutting 10.0% to **8.2%** after tax. The index fund ≈ **0.6 points**, cutting 12.3% to **11.7%**. On $10,000 the after-tax gain was $61,700 for active funds vs **$149,000** for the index fund.
- After tax *and* inflation: real after-tax wealth was $65,100 for the index fund vs $23,100 for the average active fund, nearly 3×. 1996–2005: taxes still took 1.7 points of the average fund's 8.5% return.
- **Dividend paradox:** gross yield was ≈1.8% for both (late 2006). The active fund's 1.5% expense ratio leaves only **0.3%** net: fees "confiscate fully 80 percent of its dividend income". The index fund's ≈0.15% expense ratio leaves **1.65%**. Its higher taxable dividend is the better deal.
- The index investor still owes tax on gains when selling. But shares bequeathed to heirs get a stepped-up cost basis.
- About half of equity fund shares sit in tax-deferred accounts (IRAs, 401(k)-type plans), where this chapter doesn't apply.
- William Bernstein (quoted): owning active funds in taxable accounts is "truly a terrible idea". Taxes are "a drag on performance of up to 4 percentage points each year".

## 5. The Grand Illusion: Investor Returns Trail Fund Returns [verified]

- Reported fund returns are *time-weighted*. What investors actually earn is the *dollar-weighted* return, which reflects when money flows in and out. "Money flows into most funds after good performance, and goes out when bad performance follows."
- Footnote example: a $100M fund earns 30% in a year, and $1B of new money arrives on the last day. The average investor's return is just **4.9%**.
- **1980–2005:** the index fund earned 12.3%, the average equity fund 10.0%, and the **average fund investor 7.3%**. Even index-fund investors earned 10.8%, 1.5 points short of their fund.
  - $10,000 grew to $170,800 (index fund), $98,200 (average fund), and **$48,200** (average fund investor), just 28% of the index result.
  - In real terms: $76,200 vs $16,700, or 22%.
- Two penalties: **timing** (too little invested when stocks were cheap, too much near the peak) and **selection** (piling into the riskiest funds at the wrong time).
  - Net equity-fund inflows were $18B in 1990, when stocks were cheap, vs **$420B in 1999–2000**, when stocks were overvalued.
  - Aggressive growth funds took 20% of the money in 1990 vs **95%** at the 1999–2000 peak.
  - For 198 of the 200 most popular funds of 1996–2000, investor returns were lower than reported returns over the following decade.
- **Hot-fund case (1996–2005):** popular aggressive growth funds reported **7.8%/yr**, but their shareholders earned **−0.4%/yr**, a gap of 8.3 points. Cumulatively: fund +112%, shareholders −4.5%.
- "When ever-counterproductive investor emotions are played on by ever-counterproductive fund industry promotions, little good is apt to result."
- Buffett's "four E's" (quoted): "The greatest Enemies of the Equity investor are Expenses and Emotions."

## 6. When Returns Are Lower, Costs Bite Harder [verified]

- Of the market's 12.5%/yr return over 1980–2005, about **2.7 points were speculative return**: the P/E rose from 9 to 18 (it peaked at 32 in early 2000). The investment return of 9.8% was close to the historical 9.5%.
- **Bogle's 2006 forecast** (an illustration of the method, not a prediction to reuse):
  - The dividend yield was below 2% (vs the 4.5% historical average), and earnings growth was assumed at 5–6% nominal, giving a 7–8% investment return.
  - If the P/E eases from 18 to 16, the market returns ≈ **7%**.
  - If the P/E goes to 25, add 3 points (≈11%). If it drops to 12, subtract 4 points (≈4%).
- Caveat: because companies keep issuing shares, per-share earnings growth can lag aggregate earnings growth by as much as 2 points a year.
- At a 7% market return, the average active fund nets only ≈1.4%/yr after costs, taxes, and 2.3% inflation (Bogle also cites 1.2%). That is before any timing or selection penalty.
- **Cost share rises as returns fall:** 2.5 points of costs consume about 16% of a 15% return, 25% of a 10% return, nearly 40% of a 7% return, and nearly 60% of a 4.5% real return.

## 7. Picking Winning Funds Is Looking for a Needle in a Haystack [verified]

- Of the **355 equity funds** that existed in 1970, most have since disappeared. Only **9** beat the market by more than 2 points a year over the next 35 years, and most of those lost their edge long ago. Only three of the 355 kept winning consistently.
- Bogle's estimated odds of an active manager beating the index: about 29% over 1 year, 15% over 5 years, 9% over 10, 5% over 25, and 2% over 50.
- **Reversion to the mean (RTM):** past top performers tend to fall back toward average. Fund stars "are rarely stars; all too often they are comets."
- Star ratings and past performance attract most fund inflows but don't predict future results.
- "Don't look for the needle in the haystack. Just buy the haystack!"
- **Occam's Razor:** when several solutions exist, choose the simplest one. Here that means the broad-market index fund.

## 8. Cost Is the Best Single Predictor [verified]

- "Performance comes and goes, but costs go on forever." Expense ratios, sales loads, and turnover habits all persist over time. High-cost funds stay high-cost, and load funds rarely become no-load.
- Turnover costs about 0.5% on each purchase and on each sale, so 100% turnover costs ≈1% of assets a year.
- **Equity funds sorted by all-in cost** (expense ratio + turnover cost, 1995–2005 data):

| Cost quartile | All-in cost | Gross return | Net return | Volatility | Risk-adjusted return | Cumulative risk-adjusted gain |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lowest | 0.9% | 12.6% | **11.7%** | 16.0% | 11.9% | 207% |
| Highest | 3.0% | 12.0% | **9.0%** | 21.4% | 8.1% | 118% |
| S&P 500 index fund | 0.2% | 11.4% | 11.2% | 15.7% | 11.4% | 194% |

- Gross returns were nearly identical across all quartiles (12.0–12.8%), so costs explain most of the difference in net returns. The highest-cost funds also took on **34% more risk**.
- "If investors could rely on only a single factor to select future superior performers and to avoid future inferior performers, it would be fund costs."
- "The more the managers and brokers take, the less the investors make."

## 9. Advisers and Fund Selection [verified]

- Advisers can add value: asset allocation, tax and savings planning, peace of mind, and keeping clients from "chasing past performance or trying to time the market". But there is no evidence they pick winning funds.
- **Harvard-led study (1996–2002):** equity funds held by adviser-reliant investors returned **2.9%/yr**, vs **6.6%** for funds bought directly. Underperformance of broker-sold funds cost investors about $9B a year.
- **New York Times contest (July 1993–June 2000):** five advisers each invested $50,000. Their average profit was **$88,500**, vs **$138,750** for the Vanguard 500 index fund, about 40% less.
- **Hulbert's newsletter tracking (26 years):** of the 35 newsletters that existed in 1980, only 13 survived, and only 3 beat the market. $100,000 in the S&P 500 grew to nearly $2.5M, vs about $1.4M for the newsletters' portfolios.
- **Merrill Lynch case (March 2000):** two new-economy funds gathered $2.0B at the bubble peak. Internet Strategies lost 86% and was merged away. Focus Twenty returned −79% through late 2006. "The best time to sell a new fund to investors—when it's hot—is often the worst time to buy it."
- **Fee guidance:** advisory fees usually start around 1%/yr, so weigh the services against that drag. Favor advisers who use stock and bond index funds.
- Bernstein (quoted):
  - Use a "fee-only" adviser.
  - Warning signs: load funds, insurance products, limited partnerships, separate accounts.
  - Pay no more than 1%; ≤0.75% above $1M; ≤0.5% above $5M.
  - An adviser who claims he can find managers who beat the indexes "is fooling both you and himself."

## 10. Fund and Product Evaluation Checklist

Apply these checks when evaluating any fund, ETF, or advised portfolio:

1. **All-in cost**: expense ratio + sales loads + estimated turnover cost (≈1% × turnover rate) + cash drag + tax drag. Lower is better. This is the most reliable predictor of relative returns.
2. **Breadth:** a total-market or S&P 500 index fund is the default. Narrow sector or "clever" indexes add tracking risk.
3. **Behavior:** an ETF is fine if bought and held. "Don't speculate in ETFs. Invest in them." Bogle criticizes ETFs as tools for traders.
4. **"Fundamental" or smart-beta indexing:** be skeptical. Its outperformance claims rely on past-period backtests and higher costs.
5. **Closet index funds** (track the market but charge active fees): no.
6. **Hedge funds and funds-of-funds:** no. "The hedge fund, it is said, is not an investment strategy but a compensation strategy." Funds-of-funds add another layer of fees.
7. **Commodity funds:** no. Commodities have no earnings, dividends, or interest to support their value.
8. **Investor return vs fund return:** fund investors' actual dollar-weighted returns trail the funds' reported returns because of badly timed purchases and switching (§5). Is the fund a recent hot performer or a newly launched theme fund? Those are red flags.
9. **Account location:** a high-turnover active fund in a *taxable* account adds tax drag of about 1.8 points/yr or more (§4).
10. **Adviser layer:** is the adviser fee-only, charging ≤1%? Does he recommend index funds, and avoid loads, insurance wrappers, and LPs (§9)?
11. **Return expectations:** build them from dividend yield + earnings growth ± P/E change, then subtract all costs, taxes, and inflation (§2, §6).

## 11. Portfolio Construction [verified]

- **Serious Money vs Funny Money:** keep ≥ 95% of assets in Serious Money and at least 50% (up to 100%) in classic index funds. Speculation (individual stock picks, active funds) goes in a Funny Money account, "not one penny more than 5 percent". Compare its 1-, 5-, and 10-year results against Serious Money.
- **Bonds:** index funds are also the best way for most investors to own bonds. Prefer the total U.S. bond market, intermediate term. Short-term bond funds suit those who want principal stability. Inflation-linked Treasurys protect purchasing power.
- **Asset allocation rule of thumb:** hold a bond position roughly **equal to your age** (20% at 20, 70% at 70), or your age minus 10. "There are no hard-and-fast rules here."
- **International:** foreign stocks at no more than about 20% of equities, via a low-cost total international index fund.
- **Slice-and-dice (optional):** for example, 85% core index fund, 10% value index fund, 5% small-cap index fund. This adds the risk of trailing the market.
- **Balanced and target-date index funds** put allocation "on automatic pilot" with gradual rebalancing.
- Buffett is quoted approvingly: most investors will find the best way to own common stocks is through a low-fee index fund.
- "Stay the course." Do nothing after building a sensible index portfolio.

- "We get precisely what we don't pay for."
- "The miracle of compounding returns is overwhelmed by the tyranny of compounding costs."
- "Market return, minus cost, equals investor return."
- "Don't speculate in ETFs. Invest in them."

- "The more the managers and brokers take, the less the investors make."
